name: Aaron Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the sales team at the seaside branch of a regional agency chain, four negotiators including me. A normal day is valuations in the morning, then chasing buyers' solicitors, then two or three viewings after work hours, because that's when people can come. The best bit is the call where I tell a first-time buyer their offer's accepted. The worst bit is a chain of five sales falling apart on a Friday afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you paid, and does it cover the bills?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Low basic salary plus commission, which in this town is lower than in the city because houses are cheaper. In summer I'm fine, in winter it's tight, and I've never had more than a few weeks of money saved. My partner Leila is a nurse at the district hospital, so her pay is the steady bit. I use AI now and then to tidy up a property description, but I check every word, because one wrong room size and you've got a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently. It's a handy spell-checker with a big marketing budget. At work I'd tell the team to keep using it for first drafts and stop worrying. Online I probably wouldn't say much, I'd rather post about the housing shortage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine, but my income was always the shaky part, AI or not. Commission in a seaside town swings with the season and with interest rates. One bad winter and we're on Leila's wages plus my basic, which barely covers our rent. So nothing changes, which means the worry I had last year is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling and keep the team steady. I'd try again to build up two months of savings by putting my summer commission straight into a separate account. And I'd ask the area manager about a higher basic, since I've topped the branch figures three quarters running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. It's not fear, it's the same low hum you get every November when viewings dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first in a bad winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, then my football season ticket. We've done it before. The thing I won't cut is the car, because no car means no valuations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a higher basic. What happens if the answer is no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the one other agency in town, but they pay worse. Realistically I'd stay and grumble. There aren't many places to go round here.

say: AI is a handy **spell-checker** with a big marketing budget.
The team should keep using it for **first drafts** and stop worrying.
think: My **job is fine**, but commission in a seaside town was always shaky.
One **bad winter** leaves us on Leila's wages and my basic pay.
do: **Put** summer commission straight into a separate **savings account**.
**Ask** the area manager for a higher basic after topping the branch figures.
feel: **Flat** rather than scared, like the usual **November hum** when viewings dry up.
S0.quote: Commission in a seaside town swings with the season and with interest rates, AI or not.
fieldNote: His worry is the **seasonal income** he already lives with, not the technology.
He uses AI as a **checked tool**, careful about legal complaints over room sizes.
Few local agencies mean his **bargaining power** is weak despite top figures.

steps.text: Keep running the sales team and booking evening viewings
Move summer commission into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chain will use this to cut negotiators, and staff should have a say in how it's done. I'd raise it at our team meeting and probably join a union for the first time. Online I'd say the savings should go to staff and buyers, not just shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a lot of my job is on that list. Writing listings, booking viewings, chasing solicitors, answering portal enquiries, all of that can be software. What's left is valuations and the negotiating, which I'm good at. But if each branch only needs two negotiators instead of four, I'm leading a smaller team for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the chain's AI system properly once it's rolled out, not just play with it. I'd join the union, because if they're going to cut, I want rules about how. I'd cut our spending, starting with the season ticket and the gym. And I'd start the qualification for mortgage advice, since buyers will still want a human to explain a thirty-year loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. It's like a long storm forecast; you board up the windows and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan, who's been there twenty years and still prints everything. He's great with older sellers. But he'd hate a new system, and the chain will see his salary and not his customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mortgage advice rather than something new altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to change once it's proven, not jump off a cliff. Mortgage advice sits right next to what I do, it pays a bit better, and the chain already employs advisers. It's a step sideways, not a leap.

think: Listings, bookings and **solicitor chasing** can all become software.

**Join** the union for the first time and cut the **season ticket**.
**Start** a mortgage adviser qualification as a sideways step.

S1.quote: Buyers will still want a human to explain a thirty-year loan.
fieldNote: He reads the card as a **branch shrinking** from four negotiators to two.
His steady nature shows in choosing a **sideways step** rather than a leap.
Progressive views turn into concrete **union** membership, a first for him.

steps.text: Complete the chain's AI system training once it launches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to protect people, with a wage floor and real retraining. At work I'd say let's be honest with staff now, before the chain does it by email. Online I'd be sharing union statements and probably arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think buying and selling a house becomes an app by 2028. The portals will value, list, book and chase. The bit that stays a while is the human in the room, the valuation walk-round and the hard conversation on the phone, until robots arrive in 2031. And frankly mortgage advice is thinking work too, so my sideways step is in the same fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Leila about whether we move closer to her hospital and live on her pay while I retrain for something hands-on. I'd look at a short course in building surveying or property inspection, where you're up in lofts and checking damp. I'd join the union campaign for a guaranteed income. And I'd sell my car if we moved, because I wouldn't need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, properly. Two years is less than one mortgage application cycle in some chains I've dealt with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you might be the earner for a bit, and I'm sorry. She'd say don't be daft, we've been on one wage before. But I'd see her doing the maths in her head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about hands-on work, but robots come three years later. Is that a plan or a delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delay, I know. But three years of pay is three years. And a hospital will need people longer than an estate agency will, so being near Leila's work matters.

say: Government should protect people with a **wage floor** and real retraining.
Staff deserve **honesty now**, before the chain announces cuts by email.
think: Buying and selling a house becomes **an app** by 2028.
Even my **mortgage advice** plan is thinking work, so it's in the same fire.
do: **Move** nearer Leila's hospital and live on her pay while I retrain.
**Take** a short course in **property inspection** or building surveying.
**Join** the union campaign for a guaranteed income.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years is shorter than some **property chains** take to complete.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Leila she might be the earner for a while, and I'm sorry.
fieldNote: He realises his **sideways step** is still exposed, which shakes his steady approach.
Leila's **nursing job** becomes the household anchor.
He sees the **robot gap** as a delay, not a plan, and says so.

steps.text: Move nearer Leila's hospital to live on her nursing pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan and short enough that we must start now. At work I'd push for a joint plan between staff and management. Online I'd share practical stuff, like which courses are free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me, if I'm sensible. I'd have the mortgage qualification by 2028 and use it for a few years, then shift towards inspection work before 2031. By then Leila and I might have a deposit, which is the dream. It's tight, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the mortgage adviser course on the chain's money. I'd use the AI tools every day, because if they're coming I want to be the one in the branch who knows them. I'd put any commission over a thousand pounds into savings. And I'd join the union, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. I like having a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said quietly. Why quietly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the area manager decides who goes when cuts come. I believe in unions, but I'm not stupid. I'd be a member, not a megaphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money stand by 2031 in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three months saved, if winters are kind. Not a house, but not on the edge either. Leila says I'm optimistic, and she's usually right.

Staff and management should build a **joint plan**.
think: I can get the **mortgage qualification** by 2028 and use it for a few years.
Shifting to **inspection work** before 2031 is tight but doable.

**Save** any commission over a thousand pounds.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because I like having a **timetable**.

fieldNote: He becomes **more active** with AI tools when time allows, showing steady adaptation.

He rates himself uneasy, but expects his **branch role** to shrink within five years.

steps.text: Take the mortgage adviser course paid for by the chain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, as long as people actually use it. I'd tell friends to start courses now while employers will pay. Online I'd push for training funds for workers in their twenties, not only young school leavers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine for me. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, with time to build a second career. The worry about winter commission is still there, though. AI being far off doesn't pay the December rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on selling and leading the team. I'd start a part-time surveying degree in the second year, paid in instalments. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard, no rush. And I'd keep building savings slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with the usual money hum. It's the first picture plus a long to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change any family plans with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for a flat of our own around 2029. A decade of warning makes it feel less mad to sign a mortgage. We'd also talk about kids, but not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the winter worry is still there. Does that change your mood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My job looks safe for years, but the money's still tight. So I'd say I'm uneasy, not calm.

Workers in their twenties need **training funds** too.
think: At **thirty-seven** in 2036 I'd have time to build a second career.
The **winter commission** problem still pays nobody's rent.
do: **Start** a part-time **surveying degree** in the second year.
**Learn** the AI tools as they become standard, without rushing.
**Aim** for a flat of our own around 2029.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with the usual **money hum** underneath.
S4.quote: AI being ten years off doesn't pay the December rent.
fieldNote: The long runway makes him **plan big**: a degree and a flat purchase.
He keeps the **seasonal money** worry front and centre in every scenario.

steps.text: Keep leading the sales team at the seaside branch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to finish a sideways step, and we'd be on Leila's wage. What would help is a proper income guarantee during retraining, so a couple like us doesn't burn through their only savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about buyers. Nobody trusts a house price that comes out of a machine, at least not yet. If agents vanish, someone still has to tell a nervous couple whether the survey problem is serious.

headlineQuote: Nobody trusts a house price that comes out of a machine, at least not yet.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old **sales team lead** at a regional chain's seaside branch, living with his nurse partner Leila.
His income swings with **commission** and seasons, and he's never saved more than a few weeks.
He uses AI **now and then**, checks every word, and prefers sideways steps once change is proven.
He moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, leaning on Leila's steady pay.
His plans run through **mortgage advice**, union membership and later property inspection work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to finish a sideways move.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee** during retraining so the couple doesn't burn through their only savings.
